prompt: You co-founded Y Combinator with Jessica Livingston, and press coverage keeps describing early YC as a one-man show. Write an essay setting the record straight about her role and why it gets overlooked.
Write a short essay of writing advice: why do people write so differently from how they talk, and what should they do about it?

I want an essay for startup founders about the single most important question to ask once a company is several months old: on current revenue growth and expenses, does it reach profitability before the money runs out?
You've spent years picking which early-stage startups to fund. Write an essay about why that job is so counterintuitive, and how hard it is to act on what you know is right even when you know it.

You've been running an online discussion community for two years as a side project. Write an essay on what you've learned: about growth, keeping the quality up, bad submissions and bad comments, and the people a site like that attracts.
Write an essay about how the city you live in shapes your ambitions. Do different cities push people toward different kinds of success, and how should an ambitious young person decide where to live?

Write an essay about being judged: admissions, hiring, investors, dating. Is it right to call it unfair when these decisions go against us, and how should knowing the answer change the way we handle rejection?

I'd like a light, reflective blog post built around a simple self-test for figuring out what you're actually dependent on in daily life. Use yourself as the example and be honest about what it reveals.

You just ran the first batch of a summer program that funded a handful of very young first-time founders. Write a reflective essay on what the experiment taught you about young founders, how they work, and what that suggests for the future.

You're running a summer program that funds very young startup founders, and you're reading through a couple hundred applications. A lot of them come from obviously capable people pitching weak ideas. Write an essay about why smart, technically talented people so often start with bad business ideas, drawing on your own first failed startup.

I keep seeing projects claim huge speedups over established software, and when I dig in the numbers don't hold up. Write an essay about how coding agents are changing the trustworthiness of performance benchmarks. Use an example of your own if you have one, and say what, if anything, is real underneath the hype.

Write an essay about what goes wrong when we chase intermediate measurements instead of the thing we actually care about. Pull examples from a few very different fields, including at least one from software engineering, and be concrete about how the proxy and the goal come apart in each.

Paul Graham recently wrote that convertible notes and rolling closes are replacing fixed-valuation equity rounds put together by angel syndicates. I'm a programmer and that sentence is Greek to me. Can you explain it all for a layman: what angels are, why raising from them is painful, what valuation means, and how convertible notes, discounts and valuation caps work? Use simple made-up numbers.

Some developers commenting on my last post said they don't want non-technical 'idiots' using their software anyway. I'd like to answer that. Write an essay about why customers won't ask the 'stupid' questions they have, what that costs a software seller, and what to do about it. A personal story would help.

Why do deep neural networks work so well? I'd like a blog post that tries to answer this through the lens of natural language processing results, aimed at readers who know some machine learning but haven't followed NLP research closely.

Several open source projects have asked me whether they should set up a software foundation. Write up a considered blog post on whether foundations are the right governance model for open source, and what the alternatives might look like.

Every time something terrible happens online, people demand that hosting and payment companies cut off the people involved. Write a short personal essay on why that line is harder to draw than it looks.

A Pew survey found that 40% of US millennials think the government should be able to censor speech that's offensive to minority groups, more than any other generation. That seems odd for the most online, most tolerant generation. Write a blog post trying to make sense of it.

Marco Arment funding his Overcast app through patronage set off a big argument about whether only people with famous personal brands can live off crowdfunding. Write a short essay on what crowdfunding has actually proven, and what might come after it.
I almost never use my shell's job control (fg, bg, Ctrl+Z and so on). I just open another tab. Write a blog post explaining what job control is and the real situations where it's worth using.

I've written SQL for years but I couldn't tell you in what order the clauses of a SELECT query are logically evaluated, or why I can't filter on a window function in WHERE. Write a blog post explaining the order and what it lets you reason about.

How does the `locate` command actually work, and why is it so much faster than `find`? Poke at it on a real Linux machine, see if you can build a crude version yourself, and write up what you find in a short, playful blog post.

A lot of developers I know say they'd like to blog but never start, usually for reasons I think are wrong. Write a blog post going through the beliefs that hold people back from technical blogging and why they don't hold up.

Write a blog post about what it really takes to start running a new, fairly immature piece of infrastructure software (a proxy, an orchestrator, that kind of thing) in production without causing serious outages. Draw on hands-on operations experience, and be honest about when this level of care isn't worth it.

I keep hearing that distributed systems have to trade consistency against availability, but I don't have an intuition for why. Write a beginner-friendly blog post that builds that intuition without leaning on the formal CAP theorem.

Write a blog post about announcing your plans at work before a project is done. Why does it feel so scary to tell people what you're working on, why is it worth doing anyway, and are there times keeping quiet is the right call?

How do you actually know you're getting better at programming? I'm skeptical of the usual set-goals-and-check-them approach. Write a blog post exploring a better way to notice and track your progress.

I was helping a newer programmer debug and realized I've never seen a good guide to the process of debugging itself. Write a blog post pulling together what debugging a program actually looks like, step by step, with practical advice.

I'm a parent of two toddlers and I keep seeing my own quirks, and my spouse's, reappear in them. Write a funny, affectionate personal essay about heredity and small children, and about what bedtime negotiation with a two-year-old actually looks like, including the internet's opinions on how I handle it.

I just read a novel whose heroine preaches that we should stop doomscrolling and recognize how much the world has improved. It got me thinking about the whole anti-doomerism camp. Write an essay on whether optimism-as-a-movement holds together, using the book as a way in.

Write a short, honest essay on whether it makes sense to call people genetically inferior, using something like cystic fibrosis as a test case. Then turn it around: what should I make of the feeling that someone else is simply better than me?

I've noticed that scandals and exposes seem to land on people right when they become unpopular, not when they actually did the thing. Write an essay about whether journalism targets people, using recent examples, and what that implies about how much we should update on a dramatic scandal.

I'm a rationalist-leaning blogger who just became the father of twins after some fertility worries. Write a funny, personal, ultimately moving essay about the experience, from the waiting room to the sleepless first weeks, including what I hope to pass on to my kids.

A group of long-termists, forecasters and AI-risk activists recently argued in public about whether we should pause frontier AI development, and even though they all think AI is dangerous they couldn't agree. Write a long blog post sorting out the positions, what each side gets right, and where you personally come down.

Elon Musk has said his plan for keeping a superintelligent AI safe is to make it maximally curious and truth-seeking rather than programming in a morality. I like the instinct but something feels off. Write an essay, from the viewpoint of someone who follows AI alignment closely, on whether this is a good plan.

I keep hearing people say that most self-identified bisexuals are faking it because they've only ever dated one sex. Is there a statistical reason that could be misleading? Write a thoughtful post on what we should expect from people who really are attracted to both sexes, what the evidence says, and whether the label still makes sense for them.

I've been reading about chronic fatigue syndrome and I keep wondering whether it's a new illness or something people have always had under different names. Write a book-review style essay on a history of exhaustion, tracing how each era (monks, physicians, Victorian nerve doctors, modern medicine) explained the same weariness and what that says about how we explain it now.
Tell me a short true story about a bad date that ended in minutes and what it taught you about curiosity.
Write a short, punchy manifesto on how to live, built around the idea of balance.
A friend of mine writes songs but has zero interest in performing them. What practical advice would you give someone who wants to make it as a songwriter only? Write it as a short blog post.

Why is it that I read something that feels deeply important, even life-changing, and a week later I'm back to being the same person? Write an essay about how to actually hold onto what matters, maybe drawing on how people in the past dealt with this.

Humans seem built to learn by hanging around people who are good at things, yet we educate almost everyone in schools. Could the internet let novices sit alongside experts at scale? Write a long essay exploring that, with concrete examples from anthropology and from places like open source.
Write an essay about why new platforms and networked products so often fail to get started, and what the founders who succeed do about it. Use real history from computing.

You just moved your software company into a new office you designed yourself. Write a blog post on why you care so much about office space for programmers, what you asked the architect for, and how it turned out.
Does the 'ship early and often' advice work for big, well-funded companies, or only for small ones? Write a short blog post using a recent half-baked beta launch as your example.

Why do computer science students graduate from good universities without knowing how to work on a real software project, and why do their term-length team projects so often produce nothing useful? Write it as an opinionated blog post, with a suggestion for what to do about it.

An economist argues that mental illnesses are just unusual preferences rather than real constraints, the way a physical illness is. I think that's wrong, but I want a rigorous reply. Write a response to his latest rebuttal that offers a better way to think about what makes something a disease, with concrete examples.

Around 2005 it felt like online atheism was everywhere, and now it barely registers. Write an essay about what happened to the New Atheist movement: where its energy came from, and why it faded or turned into something else.

I just read an op-ed by some economists arguing that financial incentives are much weaker than people assume, and that status and social connection matter more. Write a blog post responding to it: how much should that finding change how we think about incentives?

A friend of mine says the basic skill of rationality is believing an argument once it has been proven to you. That seems off to me but I can't say why. Write an essay on whether people should simply accept arguments they can't refute.

People throw the phrase "conspiracy theory" at everything from Russiagate to the Catholic Church abuse cover-up to climate science, and it mostly just ends discussions. Is there a principled way to tell which claims about secret coordination deserve to be taken seriously and which don't? Write an essay that tests whatever principle you come up with on a bunch of concrete cases.

Review a modern guide to Buddhist meditation written by a teacher who is also a neuroscientist. I'm interested in whether the practical advice and the brain-science model of the mind hold up, and whether its optimism about how fast people can progress is believable. Write it from the perspective of a skeptical, somewhat obsessive reader who has struggled with meditation manuals before.

I'm a doctor and patients keep asking me for notes certifying things I can't actually verify, like back pain. Write a blog post about that dilemma, what I've tried, and what it makes me think about pointless procedures in the economy.

A magazine claims Marxists never talk about incentives or the technical side of designing government because they think ideology solves everything. Write a blog post that tries to explain why people on the left and right so often talk past each other about politics, and whether the charge is fair.

Psychologists say birth order effects on personality are basically debunked. But I've noticed that in certain communities, nearly everyone seems to be an oldest child. Write a data-driven blog post taking the other side: argue that birth order effects are real, using survey data, and work through why the published research might have understated them.
